value.distinction: React supplies the component/declarative programming model; React Native applies it to native platform UI and APIs rather than browser DOM UI.
value.why_it_matters: Prevents treating the native framework as merely React DOM inside a mobile web page.

value.distinction: The source says React Native does not manipulate the DOM through the Virtual DOM and instead messages native views.
value.why_it_matters: Clarifies the rendering target and platform boundary.

value.distinction: The syntax is similar, but the source explicitly says React Native does not use CSS as its stylesheet system.
value.why_it_matters: Avoids assuming browser CSS support or identical layout behavior.

value.distinction: The source says React Native does not use HTML; View, Text and Button are framework components mapped to native UI.
value.why_it_matters: Separates browser document structure from native component composition.

value.distinction: JavaScript is the runtime language described; TypeScript adds static type annotations and is commonly used for type safety.
value.why_it_matters: Separates authoring-time type checking from runtime execution.

value.why_it_matters: Makes execution boundaries and communication mechanisms explicit.

value.why_it_matters: Prevents assuming every platform has identical features or zero native code.

value.why_it_matters: Separates extension capability from native styling semantics.

value.why_it_matters: Avoids overreading a platform list as a support-level guarantee.

value.misconception: React Native renders the application by manipulating browser DOM nodes through React's Virtual DOM.
value.correction: The supplied article explicitly contrasts React Native with DOM manipulation and describes messages updating native views.

value.misconception: React Native directly uses standard browser CSS.
value.correction: The article says the styling syntax resembles CSS but React Native does not use CSS itself; styles affect native views.

value.misconception: A React Native screen is an HTML document.
value.correction: The source says React Native does not use HTML and presents View, Text and Button as framework components.

value.misconception: Cross-platform means no native platform code or APIs are involved.
value.correction: The article says React components wrap native code and interact with native APIs.

value.misconception: Every platform listed has identical support and maintenance.
value.correction: The source lists many targets and separately identifies Microsoft as maintainer of Windows/macOS implementations; it does not claim equal support across all targets.

value.misconception: TypeScript replaces JavaScript as the runtime described by the article.
value.correction: The source describes JavaScript interpretation on device and TypeScript as a commonly used typed authoring option.

value.misconception: Props and state are interchangeable.
value.correction: Props are component inputs; state is updated by a setter such as setCount.

value.misconception: baseNumber is required in the TypeScript example.
value.correction: The question mark marks baseNumber as optional; title has no question mark and is required.

value.misconception: The article describes the JavaScript/native bridge as synchronous and unbatched.
value.correction: The source explicitly describes serialized data over an asynchronous and batched bridge.

value.misconception: The described bridge details necessarily apply identically to every React Native version and platform.
value.correction: This graph preserves the article's architecture description with a version/scope qualification; it does not assert universal implementation identity.

value.misconception: React Native is only for Android and iOS.
value.correction: The supplied article lists additional targets including desktop, TV, web, UWP, Vega OS, OpenHarmony and visionOS.

value.misconception: React and React Native are identical products.
value.correction: React provides the component/declarative model, while React Native integrates it with native platform views and APIs.

value.misconception: Open-source status and MIT license are the same type of fact.
value.correction: The article states the project is open-source and separately lists MIT as the license.

value.misconception: Version 0.87.1 was the initial React Native release.
value.correction: The article gives 2015 as the initial release date and 0.87.1 as a later stable release listed in the infobox.

value.misconception: Any performance consequence inferred from bridge serialization is a direct measured claim in the article.
value.correction: The source states serialization, asynchrony and batching; specific performance effects are explanatory hypotheses requiring workload-specific measurement.

value.misconception: Every organization listed as a user still uses React Native in the same way today.
value.correction: The article specifically notes Shopify is retiring its use, so adoption statements must preserve their time context.

value.misconception: The article's 2025 foundation announcement by itself proves every governance or transfer detail is complete.
value.correction: The supplied text reports an announcement; this graph does not independently verify its implementation status.

value.misconception: The article's citation warning proves all of its listed references are unreliable.
value.correction: The notice says some sources may be unreliable, not that every citation is invalid.

source_claims.claim: React Native is an open-source UI software framework developed by Meta and the community.
The article lists Android, Android TV, iOS, macOS, tvOS, OpenHarmony, Web, Windows, UWP, VR, Vega OS and visionOS among platform targets or application domains.
The infobox identifies the MIT License.
The infobox gives 26 April 2015 as the release date and 0.87.1 dated 26 August 2026 as the stable release.
The implementation section describes JavaScript running in a background process on the end device and communicating with native platforms through serialized data over an asynchronous batched bridge.
The article says React Native does not manipulate the DOM via the Virtual DOM.
React components wrap existing native code and interact with native APIs through React's declarative UI paradigm and JavaScript.
React Native styling syntax resembles CSS, but the article says React Native does not use HTML or CSS.
The article says TypeScript is often used over JavaScript due to increased type safety.
The history connects Facebook's dissatisfaction with its HTML5 mobile experience to an internal UI prototype and React Native's public release.
The article says React Native was already used in production for Facebook's Group App and Ads Manager by the time of the cited technical talk.
The article reports an October 2025 announcement that React, React Native, and JSX would be donated to a React Foundation under the Linux Foundation.
The article says the React Native implementations for Windows and macOS are currently maintained by Microsoft.

value.name: Router versus switch
value.router: Uses Layer-3 destination IP/prefix to forward between IP networks
value.switch: Uses Layer-2 MAC addresses to bridge frames
value.overlap: Multilayer switches can also perform Layer-3 routing

value.distinction: Routing computes/maintains route choices; forwarding applies a selected FIB entry to a packet.
Routing table holds route information; FIB is a forwarding-optimized structure derived from it.
Router primarily uses Layer-3 destination IP; switch bridges using Layer-2 MAC addresses.
Multilayer switches can route between subnets, so capabilities overlap.
Basic forwarding does not guarantee delivery; endpoints provide reliability where needed.
NAT maps addressing/connection information; the source says it is not universally regarded as a security feature.
Control plane computes route state/FIB; forwarding plane applies FIB to packets.
Static route is manually configured; dynamic route is learned through a protocol.
Default route is used when no more-specific destination entry matches.
Access serves customer/site connectivity; distribution aggregates traffic and may enforce WAN QoS.
Distribution aggregates/policies traffic; core provides high-bandwidth backbone transit.
Edge peers at network boundaries; core carries traffic between edge routers within an AS.
P is provider transit; PE connects CE and provides VPN services.
PE is provider-side; CE is customer-side edge.
Tail drop waits for a full buffer; RED/WRED can drop earlier, with WRED differentiating traffic types.
ASIC accelerates common operations; CPU handles packets/functions requiring special attention.
Wi-Fi router integrates routing, switching, and AP; a residential gateway may also integrate a modem.
Interfaces, processors, buffers, and accelerators execute work; OS/routing code supplies behavior/configuration.
Basic IP forwarding uses header addressing and usually not payload.
AS is a routing/policy domain; physical interfaces/links are the transmission substrate.

value.misconception: A router guarantees packets reach the final destination.
value.correction: A router forwards hop by hop; basic connectionless routing does not guarantee delivery.

value.misconception: Routing and forwarding are the same operation.
value.correction: Routing maintains/selects routes and builds the FIB; forwarding uses the FIB for each packet.

value.misconception: A router normally chooses routes by reading the application payload.
value.correction: Pure IP forwarding primarily uses destination IP and optional header hints, not payload.

value.misconception: The routing table and FIB are identical.
value.correction: The FIB is derived from route information and optimized for forwarding.

value.misconception: NAT is a complete security control.
value.correction: NAT is not universally recognized as a security feature; firewalling and policy are distinct.

value.misconception: All routers are ASIC appliances.
value.correction: Routers range from software/CPU systems to network processors and ASIC-assisted devices.

value.misconception: Every router needs separate Wi-Fi AP and switch hardware.
value.correction: Home Wi-Fi routers commonly integrate router, switch, and AP functions, sometimes with modem.

value.misconception: The default route is the only route in a router.
value.correction: Route tables can contain specific static/dynamic routes and a default route for unmatched destinations.

value.misconception: A router and Layer-3 switch are wholly separate capabilities.
value.correction: Multilayer switches can route between subnets.

value.misconception: More buffering removes congestion.
value.correction: Buffers are finite; queues can increase latency and queue-management policies may drop packets.

value.misconception: QoS creates additional bandwidth.
value.correction: QoS prioritizes traffic but does not create capacity.

value.misconception: The Internet has one centrally controlled router backbone.
value.correction: Major ISP systems collectively form a distributed backbone core; there is no single central backbone router.

value.misconception: Open-source router software is automatically more secure.
value.correction: The article reports a debated argument about visibility of flaws, not a universal proof.

value.misconception: Control plane and forwarding plane must be separate physical boxes.
value.correction: The article describes functional units operating simultaneously; physical separation is not required by that statement.

value.misconception: A route entry guarantees end-to-end reachability.
value.correction: A route informs a local forwarding decision; downstream failures and congestion can still interrupt delivery.

source_claims.claim: A router forwards packets between computer networks using network-layer destination information and routing information/policy.
A router is a Layer-3 device because its primary forwarding decision is based on the destination IP address.
The control plane maintains routing information and builds a FIB; the forwarding plane consults the FIB to forward packets.
Routing tables may include static, dynamic, and default routes; a default route may also be obtained by DHCP.
Connectionless router/gateway design does not assure reliable delivery; reliability is left to hosts.
Tail drop, RED, and WRED are queue-management policies used when packets arrive faster than a router can process/transmit them.
QoS classifies traffic and affects processing priority; it is important for latency-sensitive VoIP traffic.
Router implementations range from CPU/software forwarding to network processors and ASIC-accelerated hardware.
Router roles include access, distribution, core, edge, provider, provider-edge, customer-edge, interior, exterior, and border/gateway.
Routers may integrate firewall, VPN, and NAT features, but NAT is not universally recognized as a security feature.
Wi-Fi routers combine router, switch, and wireless access point functions, and residential gateways may also integrate a modem.
The article traces router precursors from NPL/ARPANET interface computers to CYCLADES, Xerox PARC, DARPA, BBN, and 1981 multiprotocol router programs.
Routers running multiple routing protocols may selectively redistribute routes between them.
Pure IP forwarding usually uses Layer-3 addresses and optional header hints, not payload inspection.
The source does not deeply specify ASIC microarchitecture, MTU/fragmentation mechanics, or specific routing algorithms.

Louis Pouzin's CYCLADES program explores datagram networking.

Ginny Travers develops the first true IP router at BBN according to the article.
Three PDP-11-based routers are in service in the experimental prototype Internet.
